title: LID — Langage d'Interrogation de Données
subtitle: Data Query Language (DQL)
description: LID (DQL) is all about querying and reading data from the database. The core command is SELECT, and it is the most powerful and most-used command in SQL. You can filter, sort, group, join, and transform data entirely within a SELECT statement — without modifying anything in the database.

sections.name: SELECT — Basic
sections.explanation: SELECT retrieves data from one or more columns in a table. Use * to select all columns, or list specific column names. The result is returned as a table of rows — called a result set.

examples.title: Select all columns from Students
examples.code: SELECT * FROM Students;
examples.explanation: Returns every column and every row from the Students table. The * means 'all columns'.

examples.title: Select only name and email
examples.code: SELECT name, email FROM Students;
examples.explanation: Returns only the 'name' and 'email' columns. Selecting specific columns is better practice than using * — faster and clearer.

examples.title: Select with a calculated column
examples.code:
SELECT
  product_name,
  price,
  price * 1.20 AS price_with_tax
FROM Products;
examples.explanation: Creates a calculated column 'price_with_tax' on the fly. The AS keyword gives it a readable name. The original data in the table is not changed.

sections.name: WHERE — Filtering Rows
sections.explanation: WHERE filters the rows returned by a SELECT (or used by UPDATE/DELETE). Only rows that match the condition are included. You can use comparison operators (=, !=, <, >, <=, >=), logical operators (AND, OR, NOT), and special keywords (IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, IS NULL).

examples.title: Find students older than 21
examples.explanation: Returns only students where age is greater than 21.

examples.title: Multiple conditions with AND / OR
examples.explanation: AND requires both conditions to be true. OR requires at least one to be true.

examples.title: IN — match a list of values
examples.code:
SELECT * FROM Employees
WHERE department IN ('IT', 'Sales', 'HR');
examples.explanation: IN is a shortcut for multiple OR conditions. Returns employees in IT, Sales, or HR departments.

examples.title: BETWEEN — range of values
examples.explanation: BETWEEN is inclusive — it includes both 10 and 100. Equivalent to price >= 10 AND price <= 100.

examples.title: LIKE — pattern matching
examples.explanation: % matches any sequence of characters (including none). _ matches exactly one character. LIKE is used for partial text matching — case sensitivity depends on the database.

examples.title: IS NULL — check for missing values
examples.explanation: You cannot use = NULL to check for NULL — you must use IS NULL. NULL means 'unknown/missing', not zero or empty string.

sections.name: ORDER BY — Sorting Results
sections.explanation: ORDER BY sorts the result set by one or more columns. ASC (ascending, smallest to largest, A to Z) is the default. DESC (descending, largest to smallest, Z to A) reverses the order.

examples.title: Sort students by age (youngest first)
examples.explanation: Results are sorted from youngest to oldest. ASC is the default so it can be omitted.

examples.title: Sort products by price (most expensive first)
examples.explanation: DESC reverses the sort — highest price appears first.

examples.title: Sort by multiple columns
examples.explanation: First sorted alphabetically by department. Within the same department, employees are sorted by salary from highest to lowest.

sections.name: LIMIT / TOP — Restricting Rows
sections.explanation: LIMIT (MySQL/PostgreSQL) or TOP (SQL Server) restricts how many rows are returned. Useful for pagination, previewing data, or finding top/bottom N records.

examples.title: Get the first 5 students
examples.code:
SELECT * FROM Students
LIMIT 5;
examples.explanation: Returns only the first 5 rows. Without ORDER BY, the order is not guaranteed — add ORDER BY to get meaningful top results.

examples.title: Top 3 most expensive products
examples.code:
SELECT product_name, price
FROM Products
ORDER BY price DESC
LIMIT 3;
examples.explanation: Sorts by price descending then takes only the top 3 — the three most expensive products.

examples.title: Pagination with OFFSET
examples.explanation: OFFSET skips a number of rows. Used for pagination — showing 10 results per page.

sections.name: DISTINCT — Remove Duplicates
sections.explanation: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result set. It compares all selected columns together — a row is considered a duplicate only if all selected columns match.
sections.syntax:
SELECT DISTINCT column1, column2
FROM table_name;

examples.title: List all unique departments
examples.code:
SELECT DISTINCT department
FROM Employees;
examples.explanation: Returns each department name only once, even if many employees share the same department.

examples.title: Unique combinations of city and country
examples.explanation: Returns unique city-country pairs. 'Paris, France' and 'Paris, USA' would both appear since the combination is different.

sections.name: Aliases — AS
sections.explanation: Aliases give a temporary name to a column or table in a query. They make results more readable and are often required when working with calculated columns or JOINs. Column aliases appear in the result headers. Table aliases shorten long table names.

examples.title: Rename columns in the result
examples.code:
SELECT
  emp_id     AS 'Employee ID',
  full_name  AS 'Full Name',
  salary     AS 'Monthly Salary'
FROM Employees;
examples.explanation: The column headers in the result show 'Employee ID', 'Full Name', 'Monthly Salary' instead of the raw column names.

examples.title: Table alias to shorten queries
examples.code:
SELECT
  s.name  AS student_name,
  s.age,
  s.email
FROM Students AS s
WHERE s.age > 20;
examples.explanation: 's' is an alias for the Students table. This is especially useful in JOINs where you reference two tables simultaneously.

examples.title: Alias on a calculated column
examples.code:
SELECT
  product_name,
  price,
  price * 0.90         AS discounted_price,
  price - (price * 0.90) AS savings
FROM Products;
examples.explanation: Both 'discounted_price' and 'savings' are calculated columns with readable aliases. They exist only in the result — the original table is unchanged.

sections.name: GROUP BY — Aggregating Data
sections.explanation: GROUP BY groups rows that share the same value in one or more columns, then applies aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) to each group. Every column in SELECT must either be in GROUP BY or wrapped in an aggregate function.

examples.title: Count students per age
examples.code:
SELECT age, COUNT(*) AS total_students
FROM Students
GROUP BY age
ORDER BY age;
examples.explanation: Groups all students by age and counts how many students share each age. COUNT(*) counts all rows in the group.

examples.title: Total sales per department
examples.code:
SELECT
  department,
  COUNT(*)          AS employee_count,
  AVG(salary)       AS avg_salary,
  SUM(salary)       AS total_payroll,
  MAX(salary)       AS highest_salary,
  MIN(salary)       AS lowest_salary
FROM Employees
GROUP BY department;
examples.explanation: For each department: counts employees, calculates average salary, sums all salaries, and shows highest and lowest salary.

examples.title: Group by multiple columns
examples.code:
SELECT
  department,
  status,
  COUNT(*) AS count
FROM Employees
GROUP BY department, status;
examples.explanation: Groups by the combination of department AND status. You'd get one row per unique (department, status) pair.

sections.name: HAVING — Filtering Groups
sections.explanation: HAVING filters groups created by GROUP BY. It's like WHERE but for groups. Use WHERE to filter individual rows before grouping, and HAVING to filter groups after aggregation. You cannot use aggregate functions in WHERE.
sections.syntax:
SELECT column, AGGREGATE_FUNCTION(col)
FROM table_name
GROUP BY column
HAVING AGGREGATE_FUNCTION(col) condition;

examples.title: Find departments with more than 5 employees
examples.code:
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS employee_count
FROM Employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
examples.explanation: First groups employees by department, then filters out departments with 5 or fewer employees. Only departments with more than 5 employees appear in the result.

examples.title: WHERE vs HAVING — used together
examples.code:
SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM Employees
WHERE status = 'active'         -- filter rows first
GROUP BY department
HAVING AVG(salary) > 3000;      -- then filter groups
examples.explanation: WHERE filters out inactive employees before grouping. HAVING then filters out departments where the average salary of active employees is 3000 or less.

examples.title: Products with total sold quantity over 1000
examples.code:
SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity) AS total_sold
FROM OrderItems
GROUP BY product_id
HAVING SUM(quantity) > 1000
ORDER BY total_sold DESC;
examples.explanation: Groups order items by product, sums quantities, then keeps only products where total sold exceeds 1000.

sections.name: INNER JOIN
sections.explanation: INNER JOIN combines rows from two tables where the join condition is matched in both tables. Rows that have no match in the other table are excluded from the result. This is the most common type of JOIN.
sections.syntax:
SELECT t1.col, t2.col
FROM table1 AS t1
INNER JOIN table2 AS t2
  ON t1.common_col = t2.common_col;

examples.title: Get orders with customer names
examples.code:
SELECT
  o.order_id,
  c.name AS customer_name,
  o.total,
  o.order_date
FROM Orders AS o
INNER JOIN Customers AS c
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;
examples.explanation: Combines Orders and Customers tables where customer_id matches. Orders with no matching customer (data error) are excluded.

examples.title: Join three tables
examples.code:
SELECT
  o.order_id,
  c.name      AS customer,
  p.product_name,
  oi.quantity
FROM Orders AS o
INNER JOIN Customers AS c  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
INNER JOIN OrderItems AS oi ON o.order_id    = oi.order_id
INNER JOIN Products AS p   ON oi.product_id  = p.product_id;
examples.explanation: Chains three INNER JOINs to show a complete view: which customer ordered which product and in what quantity.

sections.name: LEFT JOIN
sections.explanation: LEFT JOIN returns ALL rows from the left table and matching rows from the right table. If there is no match in the right table, NULL values fill the right table's columns. Used when you want to keep all records from the left table regardless of matches.
sections.syntax:
SELECT t1.col, t2.col
FROM table1 AS t1
LEFT JOIN table2 AS t2
  ON t1.common_col = t2.common_col;

examples.title: All customers, with their orders (if any)
examples.code:
SELECT
  c.name          AS customer_name,
  o.order_id,
  o.total
FROM Customers AS c
LEFT JOIN Orders AS o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
examples.explanation: All customers appear in the result. Customers who have never placed an order will show NULL for order_id and total.

examples.title: Find customers with NO orders
examples.code:
SELECT c.name
FROM Customers AS c
LEFT JOIN Orders AS o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;
examples.explanation: By filtering for IS NULL on the right table's column, you find all customers that have no orders at all. This is a common pattern.

sections.name: RIGHT JOIN
sections.explanation: RIGHT JOIN is the opposite of LEFT JOIN — it returns ALL rows from the right table and matching rows from the left table. If there is no match in the left table, NULL fills those columns. Less common than LEFT JOIN (you can usually rewrite it as a LEFT JOIN by swapping the tables).
sections.syntax:
SELECT t1.col, t2.col
FROM table1 AS t1
RIGHT JOIN table2 AS t2
  ON t1.common_col = t2.common_col;

examples.title: All orders, with customer info if available
examples.code:
SELECT
  o.order_id,
  o.total,
  c.name AS customer_name
FROM Customers AS c
RIGHT JOIN Orders AS o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
examples.explanation: All orders are shown. If an order has no matching customer (orphaned record), customer_name will be NULL.

sections.name: FULL OUTER JOIN
sections.explanation: FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables. Where there is a match, the row is combined. Where there is no match on either side, NULLs fill the missing columns. Not supported in MySQL — use a UNION of LEFT and RIGHT JOIN instead.
sections.syntax:
-- PostgreSQL / SQL Server:
SELECT t1.col, t2.col
FROM table1 AS t1
FULL OUTER JOIN table2 AS t2
  ON t1.common_col = t2.common_col;

-- MySQL workaround:
SELECT * FROM t1 LEFT JOIN t2 ON t1.id = t2.id
UNION
SELECT * FROM t1 RIGHT JOIN t2 ON t1.id = t2.id;

examples.title: All customers and all orders (matched or not)
examples.code:
SELECT
  c.name     AS customer_name,
  o.order_id,
  o.total
FROM Customers AS c
FULL OUTER JOIN Orders AS o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
examples.explanation: Customers without orders show NULL for order columns. Orders without customers show NULL for the customer name. All records from both tables appear.

sections.name: Subqueries
sections.explanation: A subquery is a SELECT statement nested inside another SQL statement. It runs first and its result is used by the outer query. Subqueries can appear in WHERE, FROM, or SELECT clauses. They are powerful for filtering, comparing, and computing derived data.
sections.syntax:
-- In WHERE:
SELECT * FROM table WHERE col = (SELECT ...)

-- In FROM (derived table):
SELECT * FROM (SELECT ... FROM table) AS alias

-- In SELECT (scalar subquery):
SELECT col, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ...) AS total FROM table

examples.title: Find students older than the average age
examples.explanation: The subquery calculates the average age first. The outer query then uses that value to filter students. The subquery returns a single value (scalar subquery).

examples.title: Find products never ordered
examples.explanation: The subquery returns all product_ids that appear in OrderItems. The outer query returns products whose ID does NOT appear in that list.

examples.title: Subquery in FROM clause (derived table)
examples.code:
SELECT department, avg_salary
FROM (
  SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
  FROM Employees
  GROUP BY department
) AS dept_stats
WHERE avg_salary > 4000;
examples.explanation: The subquery in FROM creates a temporary result set (named 'dept_stats'). The outer query then filters that derived table.

examples.title: Scalar subquery in SELECT
examples.code:
SELECT
  name,
  salary,
  (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM Employees) AS company_avg,
  salary - (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM Employees) AS diff_from_avg
FROM Employees;
examples.explanation: Adds the company average salary as a column next to each employee, and shows the difference. The subquery runs once per row.
